q: For a coil of N turns in which the flux through each turn changes by ΔΦ in time Δt, Faraday's and Lenz's laws give the induced emf as:
x: The emf equals the number of turns times the rate of change of flux, ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt; the minus sign shows Lenz's law.

q: In 0.1 s, the flux linking each of 500 turns changes by 2 × 10⁻³ Wb. What average emf appears across the coil?
x: ε = N ΔΦ/Δt = 500 × 2 × 10⁻³/0.1 = 10 V. Leaving out the number of turns gives 0.02 V.

q: A magnet is moved into a coil in the same way twice, once with 100 turns and once with 300 turns of the same size. Compared with the first coil, the emf in the second coil is:
x: The emf is N times the rate of change of flux per turn. With the same flux change and time, tripling N triples the emf.

q: A straight metal rod 1 m long moves at 10 m s⁻¹ through a uniform field of 0.05 T, with the rod, its velocity and the field mutually perpendicular. The emf between its ends is:
x: Motional emf ε = BLv = 0.05 × 1 × 10 = 0.5 V.

q: A 100-turn coil of resistance 10 Ω is part of a closed circuit. The flux through each turn changes by 0.01 Wb in 0.5 s. The induced current in the coil is:
x: ε = N ΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 0.01/0.5 = 2 V, so I = ε/R = 2/10 = 0.2 A. Stopping at the emf gives the tempting 2.

q: For a single loop, the induced emf at any instant equals the magnitude of the slope of the graph of:
x: ε = −dΦ/dt, which is the gradient of the flux–time graph. A flat part of that graph means zero emf.

q: The flux through a coil whose ends are not connected to anything is changing. Which statement is correct?
o: A current flows, but no emf is induced
Neither an emf nor a current is produced
Both an emf and a current are produced
An emf is induced, but no current flows
x: Faraday's law gives an emf whenever the flux linking the coil changes. A current needs a closed circuit, so with open ends no current flows.

q: In the equation ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt, the negative sign represents:
x: The minus sign shows that the induced emf opposes the change in flux that produces it, which is Lenz's law.

q: A steady current in coil P is suddenly switched off. In a nearby coaxial coil Q, a brief induced current flows:
o: In the opposite sense to the current that was in P
In both senses equally, so the net current is zero
Only if Q is connected to a battery
In the same sense as the current that was in P
x: The flux through Q falls. By Lenz's law the induced current tries to keep that flux, so it flows in the same sense as P's former current.

q: A bar magnet is dropped through a complete, uncut copper ring held horizontally. As it approaches the ring, its acceleration is:
x: The changing flux induces a current in the ring that opposes the magnet's motion (Lenz's law), so there is an upward force and the acceleration is less than g.

q: A metal loop is pulled out of a region of uniform magnetic field. The force on the induced current in the loop:
o: Helps the pull, drawing the loop out faster
Acts at right angles to the pull and does no work
Is zero because the field is uniform
Opposes the pull, tending to keep the loop in the field
x: Pulling the loop out reduces the flux. The induced current opposes this change, so the force on it acts against the pull.

q: A flat loop lies in the plane of this page in a magnetic field directed into the page. The field is decreasing. Seen from the front, the induced current in the loop flows:
o: Not at all, since the field is into the page
x: The induced current must make a field into the page to oppose the decrease. A clockwise current (seen from the front) gives a field into the page.

q: A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a lamp, and the lamp glows. The electrical energy in the lamp comes from the:
o: Work done by the person against the repelling force
Energy stored in the magnet, which slowly weakens
Internal energy of the copper wire
x: By Lenz's law the coil repels the magnet, so the person must do work to push it in. That work becomes electrical energy, in line with energy conservation.

q: A copper plate swinging between the poles of a strong magnet comes to rest much sooner than one swinging outside the field. This is because:
o: Eddy currents induced in the plate oppose its motion
Air resistance is larger between the poles
x: The moving plate cuts the field, inducing eddy currents. By Lenz's law these oppose the motion, damping the swing. Copper is not attracted by a magnet.

q: In a transformer, the coil that is connected to the alternating supply is called the:
x: The input coil connected to the AC supply is the primary; the output coil connected to the load is the secondary.

q: An ideal transformer takes 0.2 A from a 240 V supply and gives an output of 12 V. The secondary current is:
x: For an ideal transformer, VpIp = VsIs: 240 × 0.2 = 48 W, so Is = 48/12 = 4 A.

q: Find the output voltage of an ideal step-down transformer with turns ratio Np : Ns = 20 : 1, fed from 220 V AC.
x: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, so Vs = 220 × 1/20 = 11 V. Inverting the ratio gives 4400 V.

q: A transformer takes 500 W from the supply and delivers 450 W to its load. Its efficiency is:
x: Efficiency = output/input × 100% = 450/500 × 100% = 90%. A real transformer cannot exceed 100%.

q: The primary and secondary coils of a transformer are wound on one common iron core so that:
o: The two coils are electrically connected to each other
Nearly all the changing flux of the primary also links the secondary
Direct current can pass from one coil to the other
The core can store the electrical energy
x: The shared core guides the alternating flux from the primary through the secondary, giving good mutual induction. The coils are not electrically joined.

q: An ideal transformer with turns ratio Ns : Np = 1 : 20 is connected to 220 V AC. Its secondary is connected to an 11 Ω resistor. The current in the primary is:
x: Vs = 220/20 = 11 V, so Is = 11/11 = 1 A. Power is conserved, so Ip = Is × Ns/Np = 1/20 = 0.05 A.

q: Making the iron core of a transformer from thin insulated laminations mainly reduces the energy lost through:
o: Leakage of flux out of the core
x: Insulated laminations break up the paths of eddy currents in the core. Winding heating is reduced by thick wire and hysteresis by using soft iron.

q: Power sent along a line is P = VI. For a fixed power, raising the transmission voltage makes the line current:
x: I = P/V, so for the same power a higher voltage means a smaller current.

q: A power of 100 kW is transmitted at 10 kV through cables of total resistance 5 Ω. The power lost as heat in the cables is:
A grid line's voltage is raised from 11 kV to 132 kV while the same power flows through the same cables. The heat loss in the cables becomes:
x: The voltage rises 12 times, so the current falls to 1/12. Loss = I²R, so it falls to (1/12)² = 1/144.

q: Electrical power is distributed as AC rather than DC mainly because AC:
o: Has no heating effect in the cables
Can be stepped up and down easily with transformers
Needs no return path to complete the circuit
x: Transformers only work with changing current, so AC voltage can be raised for transmission and lowered for use. AC still heats cables.

q: A 20 kW supply is sent at 1000 V through cables of total resistance 2 Ω. What percentage of the power is lost as heat in the cables?
x: I = 20000/1000 = 20 A; loss = I²R = 400 × 2 = 800 W, which is 800/20000 = 4% of the power.

q: The correct order in which electricity passes from a power station to a home is:
o: Generator, step-down transformer, transmission lines, step-up transformer
Generator, transmission lines, step-up transformer, step-down transformer
Generator, step-up transformer, transmission lines, step-down transformer
Generator, step-up transformer, step-down transformer, transmission lines
x: Voltage is raised by a step-up transformer at the station, carried on the lines at high voltage, and lowered by step-down transformers near homes.

q: A transmission line of resistance 4 Ω carries a current of 25 A. The voltage lost along the line is:
x: Voltage drop = IR = 25 × 4 = 100 V. Higher transmission voltage means less current, so less voltage is lost along the line.
